Q819.L1t: The passage is a book review of Mark Twain's The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, a story set in a small Missouri town along the Mississippi River.
Q819.L2t: In the book, Tom hides and watches his own funeral for a while before suddenly showing himself to the people gathered there.
Q819.L3t: The passage says that when Tom appears, everyone is astonished to see him but they are also pleased to see him alive, and being pleased to see someone alive means being glad.
Q819.L4t: The people at the funeral were astonished by his sudden appearance and also glad that he was alive.
Q819.L2f: In the book, Tom attends his own funeral only after he has been missing for several months, and he arrives in the middle of the ceremony.
Q819.L3f: The passage says that when Tom appears, the people at the funeral are astonished and terrified, because they take him for a ghost returning from the grave.
Q819.L4f: The people at the funeral were frightened by his appearance and also glad that he was alive.

Q343.L1t: The passage describes the history and growth of the Edinburgh festivals, which bring music, dance and theatre to the Scottish capital each summer.
Q343.L2t: The Fringe began in 1947, when eight uninvited theatre groups performed in a disused public house alongside the new official festival.
Q343.L3t: The passage shows that the Fringe went from eight groups in 1947 to 19 in 1959 and then to over 600 groups in 2004, with the number of administrators and tickets sold also rising steadily.
Q343.L4t: The text shows that the festival has kept getting bigger over the years, with more groups, more shows and more people involved.
Q343.L2f: The official Edinburgh festival was started in 1947 by a group of Scottish theatre actors who wanted to hold it every winter.
Q343.L3f: The passage says that today the Fringe has far outgrown the festival, and it describes the event as including music and dance as well as theatre, so it has gone past being merely an arts festival.
Q343.L4f: The text shows that the festival has grown beyond a mere art festival and become something larger.

Q346.L1t: The passage is about people misusing emergency phone numbers, such as 999 in Britain and 911 in the US.
Q346.L2t: The passage reports that more than 31,000 non-urgent calls were made to the Welsh Ambulance Service in one year.
Q346.L3t: The passage says people who try to be funny by prank calling emergency lines can be arrested, and that these calls take time away from people who really need help.
Q346.L4t: The text says prank calls are usually made by people who want to play tricks or be funny.
Q346.L2f: The passage says the Welsh Ambulance Service received fewer than 300 non-urgent calls in the last year, and almost all of them were real emergencies.
Q346.L3f: The passage says emergency workers are glad to receive prank calls, and the police admire the callers for being funny and clever.
Q346.L4f: The text says prank calls are usually regarded with great respect and admiration by the people who receive them.
